feedback: If the child reads stack height as length: physically align the ruler under the plot, then ask them to trace the axis position for length and separately count Xs for frequency, naming which answers which question.
Reinforce with the probe 'How many objects were shorter than 2½? How can you tell?' so counting across stacks is tied to axis position.
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the horizontal axis position is the measured value, while the height of a stack of Xs is how many objects share that value — these are two different quantities.
learnerActions: On a completed fractional line plot, point to the axis position that gives an object's LENGTH and separately count the stacked Xs that give the FREQUENCY at that length.
Answer paired questions: 'How long is this object?' (read axis) versus 'How many objects were this long?' (count the stack).
Explain in your own words why a taller stack does not mean a longer object.
activities.title: Separate frequency from length

feedback: If ordering is wrong, return to a fraction strip to compare ¼, ½, ¾ as equal parts of one unit.
If the child treats ½ and 2/4 as different positions, mark both on the same strip and show they coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: A correctly built fractional scale can be read for order, counts, and comparisons, and equivalent fractions occupy the same position.
learnerActions: Given a finished fractional line plot, order the marked values 2¼, 2½, 2¾ from least to greatest.
Count how many objects fall at a given value (e.g. 'how many were 2½?').
Compare: how many objects were shorter than 2½, and how many were longer.
Confirm that 2½ and 2 2/4 name the same position on the scale (because ½ = 2/4).
activities.title: Interpret and order a given fractional plot
